rules.baseline_ovr_target: 68-72, centered near 70, derived from active Madden 27 baseline dataset

offense.question: What is a "hot read" for a quarterback?
options: A run-check call at the line of scrimmage
The receiver to throw to immediately if a blitzer beats the protection
The offense's cadence call
A formation shift before the snap

offense.question: On an outside zone run, which way is the offensive line trying to move the defensive front?
options: Straight back off the ball
Laterally toward the play side, sealing defenders to open a cutback lane
Backward into their own end zone
It doesn't matter, linemen just block whoever's in front of them

offense.question: On a "zone read," what determines whether the QB hands the ball off or keeps it?
options: The play clock
The safety's pre-snap depth
The reaction of the deliberately unblocked backside defender (usually the end)
The center's snap count

offense.question: What's the core difference between man and zone pass protection?
options: Man assigns each blocker a specific defender wherever he goes; zone assigns each blocker an area and they pass rushers between them
Zone protection is illegal on 3rd down
Man protection needs eight blockers minimum
There's no real difference between them

offense.question: What's the design purpose of a "levels" passing concept (routes stacked at different depths on the same vertical stem)?
options: To draw an illegal-formation penalty
To create a high-low read that isolates one underneath defender, forcing him to choose which route to take away
It only works when the offense blitzes itself with extra rushers
It requires no actual route combination, just depth

offense.question: What's a "sight adjustment" between a QB and receiver?
options: A pre-agreed route change based on the coverage shown, made without a verbal call
A formal challenge to the officials
A mid-play substitution
A penalty for illegal motion

offense.question: What does "max protect" mean in a play call?
options: Every eligible receiver runs a route
Extra blockers (RB/TE) stay in to pass-protect, leaving fewer receivers in routes
It's another name for a screen pass
The QB is required to run

offense.question: What does a run-pass option (RPO) let the offense do?
options: Snap the ball without a full offensive line
Let the QB decide post-snap to hand off or throw based on a defender's reaction, without changing the blocking
Only be run on 3rd and long
Guarantee a first down by rule

offense.question: What's a "switch release" between two receivers at the snap?
options: Both receivers line up in the wrong spot and the play is whistled dead
The two receivers cross paths releasing off the line, swapping which one ends up on the route breaking inside vs. outside
A substitution made only between plays, never at the snap
A blocking scheme with no route-running component at all

offense.question: In offensive line combo-block terminology, an "Ace" call is a double team between which two blockers?
options: The two tackles
The center and one guard
A guard and the tight end
Both guards

defense.question: What's the difference between a "3-technique" and a "1-technique" defensive tackle alignment?
options: 3-technique lines up on the guard's outside shoulder; 1-technique lines up on the center's outside shoulder — different gaps, different jobs
They're both linebacker alignments, not line techniques
A 1-technique always blitzes off the edge
There's no real difference between the two

defense.question: What is the "Mike" linebacker's core job in most base defenses?
options: Cover the deep middle of the field exclusively
Play the middle, read run/pass keys off the center and guards, and often make the defensive calls
Rush the passer on every snap
Cover kickoffs only

defense.question: What is "pattern matching" (match coverage), as opposed to traditional spot-drop zone?
options: Defenders start from zone-like landmarks but convert to man coverage based on the actual routes receivers run, blending zone structure with man leverage
Another name for a standard Cover 3 shell
A rule used only to defend running plays
A scheme that removes the need for a pass rush

defense.question: What's the basic deep-zone split in a "Cover 3" shell?
options: Two defenders splitting the field into halves
Three defenders each covering a third of the field
One defender covering the entire deep field alone
No deep defenders at all

defense.question: What does "run fit" refer to on defense?
options: How the team's pads fit under uniform rules
Each defender's assigned gap so the ball carrier can't find a clean running lane
The huddle formation before a play
The name of a specific blitz package

defense.question: What's distinct about defensive line assignments in a 3-4 versus a 4-3?
options: 3-4 linemen never engage a blocker
3-4 linemen more often "two-gap," controlling both gaps around the blocker in front of them to free up the linebackers
There are no defensive linemen in a 3-4
3-4 linemen blitz on every down by rule

defense.question: What's the core difference between man and zone coverage for a cornerback?
options: Man assigns the corner to a specific receiver wherever he goes; zone assigns him an area to cover whoever enters it
Zone coverage isn't legal in the NFL
Man coverage can only be played on 3rd down
There's no real difference

defense.question: What is a "Cover 4" (quarters) shell primarily built to defend?
options: The run, exclusively
Deep passing routes, splitting the deep field into four zones between two safeties and two corners
Screen passes only
Nothing — it's purely a run-blitz call

defense.question: What's a "spy" in pass defense?
options: A defender who rushes the passer immediately on every snap
A defender (often a linebacker) assigned to shadow a mobile QB and react if he scrambles, instead of covering a receiver or rushing
A coach who charts opposing tendencies from the booth
The player who calls the defensive signals only

defense.question: In a "Tampa 2" defense, which defender drops into coverage that a standard Cover 2 doesn't ask him to?
options: The strong safety
The middle (Mike) linebacker, dropping to a deep-middle zone that bridges the two deep safeties
The nose tackle
The punter
